title: A site for a product that is still private
metaTitle: A waitlist page that explains itself
excerpt: A waitlist page should say who the product is for and what they will be able to do. An email field alone collects addresses you cannot use well.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads, objects shown before their use is explained.
caption: Objects on a table, still waiting for an explanation. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What must a waitlist page say?
faqs.answer: It must say who the product is for and what those people will be able to do, in verbs, before the email field. A limit is useful when the absence would surprise someone. A logo and a form, with the explanation hidden, collects addresses you cannot write to well.

faqs.question: What should the waitlist form ask?
faqs.answer: Ask for the email and one question that helps you reply, such as the job they want done first. Say whether they will get a single launch note or an ongoing letter. Confirm on the page and in a mail they can answer.

faqs.question: What should you avoid promising on a waitlist?
faqs.answer: Avoid a date you do not control, features you do not intend to ship first, and special pricing you have not defined. Promise only the note you described on the page. If you asked a question on the form, use the answer when you write back.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A waitlist landing page has to say who the product is for and what those people will be able to do. An email field with a logo collects addresses you cannot use, because you will not know why they signed up or what to tell them when you write back. The page is a promise about a future product. The promise has to be specific enough to deserve the address.

Privacy is not an excuse for emptiness. You can be early and still be clear. You should not be early and theatrical.

## Who it is for

Name the person in the first screen. Not "teams," unless you truly mean every team. The clinic manager, the independent bookseller, the trading desk of three people. The narrower line will attract fewer emails and better ones. You want the better ones. A thousand addresses from curious generalists will not become a launch. They will become a newsletter you dread.

Say who it is not for, in a sentence, if the confusion is likely. "This is not a personal budgeting app" saves you a wave of the wrong users and saves them a disappointment. The sentence is part of the product definition. If you cannot say who it is not for, you may still be guessing the job. Go settle that before you collect mail.

Use their words if you have heard them. The phrase a buyer used on a call is a better headline than a category you invented to sound large. The page is for the person you hope to serve, not for the investor who wants the category to be big. You can explain the category in a second paragraph. The first line is the person and the job.

If you are embarrassed to be specific because the product might change, write the current intention and date it in a quiet way. "We are building this for X, and the first version will do Y." You are allowed to learn. You are not allowed to collect emails under a blank flag and later announce a product those people did not ask for. That is how a list becomes angry.

## What they will be able to do

Describe the ability in verbs. Send, reconcile, publish, book, see the position, share the file with the client. Three verbs is plenty. A taxonomy of the whole platform is a later site.

Put the verbs above the form. The form is the ask. The verbs are the reason. A form at the top, with the explanation below a fold on a phone, inverts the decision. People will submit out of habit and then not remember you, or they will leave because there was nothing to judge.

Say what the first version will not do, if the absence is surprising. "You will be able to send the packet. You will not yet have a client portal." That sentence filters the people who needed the portal and respects the people who stay. It also keeps your future launch honest, because you have already said the limit in public.

Show a fragment if you can do it without pretending the product is finished. A single real screen, cropped, with sample data that is obviously sample. Or a short sequence of the job in type, if a picture would overclaim. Do not commission a cinematic product film for a product that does not open. The film will be more specific than the software, and the software will look like a disappointment when it arrives.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the constraint on this page. People often leave in the first 10 to 20 seconds, and the value has to be clear within about 10 seconds if you want a longer look. A waitlist that spends those seconds on a riddle will lose the person who would have been a good user. Say the person and the verb immediately. Mystery is a brand costume. It does not fill a useful list.

## The form

Ask for the email and one question that helps you write back. The question might be the size of their team, the tool they use today, or the job they want done first. One question. A ten-field survey on a waitlist is a product you have not earned the right to give them.

Say what the mail will be. "We will write when the first version is ready for this kind of team, and we will not add you to a weekly letter." Then do that. If you want a letter, say there is a letter, and make it optional. Mixing a product waitlist and a marketing newsletter without saying so is how people mark you as spam and miss the one mail that mattered.

Confirm the signup on the page. Tell them it worked, repeat what they will be able to do, and tell them there is nothing else to do tonight. A confirmation email should exist, from an address you can receive replies on. Some of the best early users will reply to that mail with a paragraph. Read those. They are the research you did not schedule.

Store the answer to the extra question with the address. A spreadsheet is enough at the start. The point is that when you open the list in two months you can see who the booksellers were. A column of bare emails is a number. It is not a group you can invite well.

Do not add a referral gimmick unless you mean it. "Share to move up the list" manufactures noise and tells serious people that access is a contest. If you need a few design partners, say "reply if you want to try an early version" and choose them yourself.

## How much to show while it is private

Show the job, the person, and the limit. Hide the internal architecture, the unreleased pricing if it is fiction, and the roadmap of everything you hope to become. A private product still has a public explanation. The explanation is not the backlog.

If a screenshot would reveal a customer's data, do not use it. If it would reveal a mechanism you are not ready to support, describe the outcome instead. "You will see which invoices are waiting" does not require a picture of a dashboard you will redesign next week. A picture you will contradict is worse than no picture. People remember pictures.

A password-protected preview is reasonable for design partners. It is a poor substitute for the public page. The public page is how a stranger judges whether to ask for the password. Give them enough to ask well.

Hanabi's own public work, such as the Trade Moai trading interface concept, is allowed to be a concept because it is labeled by what it is. Your waitlist should be just as clear about its status. "In private use with a few teams" is a status. "The future of work" is not a status. Use the plainer one.

## The note you send later

Write the launch note when you write the page, even if you only save it as a draft. If you cannot draft it, the page is too vague to collect mail against. The note should remind them of the verb they signed up for, say what is now true, and give one action. It should not introduce a different product and call it "as promised."

Segment the note if you asked the extra question. The booksellers get the bookseller version. The people who wanted a different job get an honest note that this version is not for them, or they get silence if you promised silence. Do not blast a single triumphant essay to a mixed list and hope.

Send it from a person, with a way to reply. Early users are forgiving of rough edges and unforgiving of a no-reply launch. The page created an expectation of a conversation, because the product was not yet a button they could press. Honor that for the first mail at least.

If the product slipped, write that too, briefly, to the people who have been waiting longest. A waitlist is a relationship. Disappearing for a year and returning with a "we're back" is how the list dies. You do not owe them a monthly diary. You owe them the mail you described on the page.

## What not to promise

Do not promise a date you do not control. "Spring" becomes a grievance. "We will write when the first version can do these three things" is a promise you can keep. If you need a date for your own planning, keep it internal until it is close and real.

Do not promise features in order to juice the form. Every verb on the page is a commitment to the people who believed it. Put only the verbs you intend to ship in the first version. The rest is a later page, for when they are true.

Do not promise exclusivity, lifetime pricing, or a founding-member status unless you have decided the terms and can live with them. Those offers are contracts. A sentence on a landing page is a sloppy contract. If you mean to give the first twenty teams a lower price, write the number, the duration, and the limit, and keep a record of who was told.

Do not collect emails you have no plan to store carefully. Say who can see the list, and do not paste it into a tool you do not control "just for a look." The page is small. The trust is the whole product at this stage.

A useful page can be published in a short time: one screen, one form, one confirmation. It does not need a blog, a login, or a second visual system. It needs the sentence. When that sentence has to arm a sales conversation you do not yet have the team for, the page changes shape again. That piece is next: [designing for a sales team that did not exist yet](/blog/designing-for-a-sales-team-that-did-not-exist-yet).
